slides.0.title: How Champagne is made: the traditional method
slides.0.subtitle: The whole process from pressing to closing
slides.1.title: What is the traditional method?
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Second fermentation in the very bottle you buy
slides.1.highlights.0.content: A still base wine is bottled with sugar and yeast and refermented in bottle, trapping the carbon dioxide inside
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Required for Champagne
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Champagne's AOC requires it; other regions using the same method (Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta and others) may not say "méthode champenoise" and use terms such as méthode traditionnelle
slides.1.highlights.2.title: About 5–6 bar of pressure
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Comité Champagne: 5–6 bar inside the bottle, roughly three times a car tyre, which is why thick glass and a strong closure are needed
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Flavour built by time
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Dead yeast cells break down (autolysis), adding bread, brioche and nutty flavours and finer bubbles, the heart of the style
slides.1.content: In one line: base wine → second fermentation in bottle → lees ageing → disgorgement → dosage and closure.
slides.2.title: Part one: from grapes to a blended base wine
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Hand harvest and whole-bunch pressing
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Hand harvesting is required and bunches are pressed whole; gentle, fast pressing keeps colour from black grapes out of the juice
slides.2.highlights.1.title: First fermentation
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Each plot, grape and year is fermented separately in stainless steel and, in part, oak; whether to run malolactic fermentation (MLF) is a style decision
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Assemblage (blending)
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Base wines from many grapes, plots and years are blended into a consistent house style; NV relies on this above all
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Reserve wines
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Wines from earlier years are kept back and added to blends to cover weaker vintages and keep style steady; details and rules come in Level 2
slides.2.content: The base wine is usually high in acid, low in alcohol and not very pleasant to drink; the magic happens in the second half.
slides.3.title: Part two: bottle fermentation to closure
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Tirage (bottling)
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The base wine is bottled with liqueur de tirage (sugar, yeast, fining agent) under a crown cap or cork; roughly 4 g/L sugar gives 1 bar, and about 24 g/L is a common textbook figure, though houses differ
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Second fermentation and lees ageing
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Fermentation adds roughly 1.2–1.3% abv (approximate) and creates the bubbles; bottles then rest horizontally on their lees. NV needs at least 15 months from bottling, Vintage at least 36 months
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Remuage and dégorgement
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Riddling brings the sediment into the neck (by hand or in a gyropalette), then the neck is frozen and the cap removed so the plug of ice and lees is expelled
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Dosage and closure
slides.3.highlights.3.content: The topping-up liquid, liqueur d'expédition (wine and sugar), sets final sweetness, then the cork and wire cage (muselet) are applied
slides.3.content: Full order: pressing → first fermentation → blending → tirage → second fermentation → lees ageing → riddling → disgorgement → dosage → closure.
slides.4.title: Comparing other sparkling methods
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Charmat / tank method
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Second fermentation in a sealed tank, then filtering and bottling, preserving fresh fruit at lower cost; Prosecco is the classic example
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Transfer method
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Bottle fermentation, but the wine is emptied into a tank and filtered before rebottling, skipping riddling; used for some large formats and regions
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Ancestral method
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Bottled before the first fermentation ends and finished in bottle without added sugar or yeast; often cloudy and slightly sweet (pét-nat)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Others using the traditional method
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Crémant (eight French AOCs), Cava, Franciacorta, Trentodoc, English sparkling and more; Loire Crémant ageing rules versus Champagne are in the Loire course, and the global comparison is in Level 3
slides.4.content: A staple of D5: say where the second fermentation happens, whether there is filtering or riddling, and what that does to style.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the key difference between the traditional method and Charmat?
A. The traditional method re-ferments in bottle, Charmat in a tank
B. The traditional method has no second fermentation
The key is the vessel for the second fermentation: bottle versus tank.
Which is the correct order of steps?
D. Tirage → second fermentation → lees ageing → disgorgement → dosage
Dosage comes after disgorgement and sets final sweetness.
Roughly what pressure is in the bottle after second fermentation?
Comité Champagne: 5–6 bar, about three times a car tyre.
